summary.text: The bias of an estimator is the difference between its expected value and the true value of the parameter being estimated.
An estimator with zero bias is called unbiased, and all else equal it is preferable, though biased estimators with small bias are frequently used.
Bias is a distinct concept from consistency, and being unbiased does not imply the smallest mean squared error.

items.prompt: A box holds tickets numbered from 1 up to some unknown top number. You draw one ticket and use its number as your guess for the top number. What is wrong with that guess?

options.label: On average it runs too high
It is right on average, so nothing is wrong
It cannot be computed from one draw
On average it falls well below the real top number

items.explain: The expected value of the drawn number is only (n + 1)/2, so the guess is certain only to be at least as small as n and is probably too low.

items.prompt: A bathroom scale, weighing a 70 kg person many times, averages 72 kg. How does the idea of bias describe this?

options.label: Its expected reading exceeds the truth by 2 kg, so it is biased
It is unbiased, because its readings vary from weighing to weighing
It is unbiased, since 72 is close enough to 70
It is biased only if every single reading is 72

items.explain: Bias is the difference between the expected value and the true value, and an estimator with zero bias is called unbiased.

items.prompt: An estimator homes in on the true value as the sample grows. Must it also be unbiased?

options.label: Yes, converging means its bias is zero
Yes, but only once the sample is very large
No, such an estimator may be biased or unbiased
No, such an estimator is always biased

items.explain: Consistent estimators converge in probability to the true value but may be biased or unbiased, so bias is a separate concept.

items.prompt: The sample variance uses a sample mean estimated from the same data, so it runs low on average. How is it corrected?

options.label: Dividing it by n/(n−1)
Multiplying it by n/(n−1)
Adding the sample mean back in
Using a much smaller sample

items.explain: The estimator is biased downward because the sample mean comes from the same data, and multiplying by n/(n−1), Bessel's correction, makes it unbiased.

items.prompt: An estimator underestimates the true value exactly as often as it overestimates it. What property does that describe?

options.label: Mean-unbiasedness, from zero expected error
Median-unbiasedness, with its median at the true value
Consistency, from converging on the truth
Minimum mean squared error

items.explain: An estimate is median-unbiased when the median of its distribution sits at the true value, so it underestimates just as often as it overestimates.

items.prompt: An estimator is mean-unbiased for some quantity. Is an estimate of a non-linear transformation of that quantity, such as its square, guaranteed to be mean-unbiased too?

options.label: Yes, since unbiasedness carries through any change
Yes, but only for squares
No, mean-unbiasedness is not preserved under such transformations
No, but median-unbiasedness fails there too

items.explain: Mean-unbiasedness is not preserved under non-linear transformations, though median-unbiasedness is.

paragraphs.heading: What bias means
paragraphs.text: The bias of an estimator is the gap between the value it gives on average, called its expected value, and the true value of the parameter it is trying to estimate. The average here is taken over all the observations that could possibly turn up. An estimator with zero bias is called unbiased. In statistics, bias is an objective property of the estimator itself.

paragraphs.heading: The sample variance
paragraphs.text: One example is the sample variance. The naive version, which divides by n, comes out too low on average, because the sample mean it relies on is worked out from the same data. Multiplying it by n/(n−1), a fix known as Bessel's correction, gives an unbiased estimator.

paragraphs.heading: Bias and consistency
paragraphs.text: Bias is a separate idea from consistency. A consistent estimator converges in probability to the true value of the parameter, and it may be biased or unbiased. An unbiased estimator does not always exist. For instance, if a binomial random variable has parameter p, no unbiased estimator exists for 1/p.

paragraphs.heading: Transforming an estimate
paragraphs.text: Unbiasedness does not always carry over when you transform an estimate. If θ̂ is an unbiased estimator of θ, then g(θ̂) is not guaranteed in general to be unbiased for g(θ), unless g is a linear function. So mean-unbiasedness is lost under non-linear transformations.

paragraphs.heading: Tickets in a box
paragraphs.text: The bias of maximum-likelihood estimators can be large. Suppose tickets numbered 1 to n sit in a box, and you draw one at random and read its number, X. If n is unknown, the maximum-likelihood estimate of n is simply X, even though X is only (n + 1)/2 on average. All you know for certain is that n is at least X, and it is probably more. The natural unbiased estimator here is 2X − 1.

paragraphs.heading: Median-unbiased estimators
paragraphs.text: Bias can also be measured against the median instead of the mean. An estimate is median-unbiased if the median of its distribution sits at the true value, so it underestimates just as often as it overestimates. Such estimators stay median-unbiased under one-to-one transformations. They also exist in some cases where neither a mean-unbiased nor a maximum-likelihood estimator can be found.
